passages.title: How Beavers Build a Dam
passages.text: First, beavers cut down small trees with their sharp teeth. Next, they drag the branches into a stream. Then they pile up the sticks and pack mud between them. Finally, the water rises behind the dam and makes a calm pond. The beavers build a home called a lodge in the middle of the pond.

passages.title: Beavers and Muskrats
passages.text: Beavers and muskrats are both rodents that live near water. Both animals are good swimmers, and both build homes called lodges. However, they are not the same size. A beaver can weigh more than 40 pounds, but a muskrat weighs only about 3 pounds. Unlike a beaver, a muskrat has a thin tail that is flat on the sides. A beaver has a wide, flat tail.

passages.title: What a Beaver Pond Does
passages.text: When beavers build a dam, the stream slows down and spreads out. Because the water is calm, a pond forms. As a result, many new animals come to live there. Frogs lay eggs in the still water. Ducks find food and safe places to rest. The pond also soaks up rain, so the land nearby stays wet even in dry summers.

parts.answer: Beavers build a dam across a stream

parts.label: Effect
parts.answer: A calm pond forms

passages.title: The Lunchroom Problem
passages.text: Oak Street School had a big problem. Every day, the lunchroom trash cans filled up with bottles and paper. To solve the problem, the students made three bins. One bin was for cans and bottles. One bin was for paper. The last bin was for food scraps. The students made signs to help everyone sort. As a result, the school threw away half as much trash.

passages.title: How Paper Is Recycled
passages.text: Old paper can become new paper. First, a truck picks up old paper from homes and schools. Next, workers sort the paper at the recycling center. Then machines mix the paper with water to make a soft mush. After that, the mush is pressed flat and dried. Finally, the new paper is rolled up and sent to stores.

passages.text: A recycling center is a place where used things get a new life. It has many parts. For example, it has a big room where workers sort cans, bottles, and paper. passages.title: All About Triangles
passages.text: A triangle is a flat shape with three sides. It also has three corners, called angles. Triangles come in many kinds. For example, an equilateral triangle has three sides that are the same length. A right triangle has one square corner. You can find triangles in many places, such as roof tops, pizza slices, and yield signs.

passages.title: Squares and Rectangles
passages.text: Squares and rectangles are alike in many ways. Both shapes have four sides. Both also have four square corners. However, their sides are different. A square has four sides that are all the same length. A rectangle has two long sides and two short sides. Every square is a special kind of rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

passages.text: Leo had a problem. He wanted to put a rug on his bedroom floor, but he did not know what size to buy. To solve the problem, he measured the floor. It was 10 feet long and 8 feet wide. He multiplied 10 times 8 to find the area. The floor was 80 square feet. As a result, Leo bought a rug that fit.

passages.title: Kinds of Clouds
passages.text: Clouds come in many shapes. One feature of all clouds is that they are made of tiny drops of water or bits of ice. For example, cumulus clouds look like puffy cotton balls. Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, and they float very high in the sky. Stratus clouds are flat and gray. They can cover the whole sky like a blanket.

passages.title: Why Thunder Booms
passages.text: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity in a storm. It is very hot, so it heats the air around it very fast. Because the hot air spreads out quickly, it makes a loud boom. That boom is thunder. Light travels faster than sound. As a result, we see the lightning flash before we hear the thunder.

parts.answer: Lightning heats the air very fast

passages.title: Keeping Streets Dry
passages.text: Heavy rain is a problem in many cities. Streets and sidewalks do not soak up water, and the rain floods the roads. One solution is a rain garden. A rain garden is a low spot filled with plants. The plants and soil soak up rain from nearby roofs and streets. As a result, less water floods the roads, and the garden helps bees and birds too.

parts.label: Problem
parts.answer: Rain floods city streets

parts.label: Solution
parts.answer: Plant rain gardens

parts.label: Result
parts.answer: Less water floods the roads

passages.title: Shield Volcanoes
passages.text: A shield volcano is a wide, gently sloping mountain built by many layers of lava. One feature that makes it unusual is its shape: from the air, it looks like a warrior's shield lying on the ground. Its lava is thin and runny, and it can travel many miles before it cools and hardens. In addition, shield volcanoes usually erupt gently rather than explosively. They are found in places such as Hawaii, Iceland, and the Galapagos Islands. Mauna Loa in Hawaii, for example, is the largest active volcano on Earth.

parts.answer: Shield volcanoes

passages.title: Why Volcanoes Erupt
passages.text: Deep underground, intense heat melts rock into magma. Because magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, it slowly rises toward the surface. Gases, including water vapor and carbon dioxide, are dissolved in the magma. As the magma rises, pressure drops, and these gases form bubbles. If the gas pressure builds faster than it can escape, the rock above cracks. As a result, magma bursts out as lava, ash, and gas. Therefore, scientists watch gas levels closely to help predict eruptions.

parts.label: Cause
options: Gas pressure builds up in rising magma
parts.answer: Gas pressure builds up in rising magma

parts.label: Effect
options: Magma bursts out as lava, ash, and gas
The gases turn into solid rock
parts.answer: Magma bursts out as lava, ash, and gas

parts.label: Another effect
options: Scientists watch gas levels to predict eruptions
parts.answer: Scientists watch gas levels to predict eruptions

passages.title: How a Volcanic Island Forms
passages.text: Many islands in the Pacific Ocean began as volcanoes on the sea floor. First, magma pushes up through a crack in the ocean crust. Next, lava erupts and cools quickly in the cold water, forming rounded rock. Then, over thousands of years, layer after layer of lava builds an underwater mountain. After the mountain breaks the surface, waves and weather slowly wear down the new rock into soil. Finally, seeds carried by wind, birds, and ocean currents arrive, and plants take root.

passages.title: Athens and Sparta
passages.text: Athens and Sparta were both powerful city-states in ancient Greece. Both spoke Greek, worshipped the same gods, and joined forces to fight the Persian Empire. However, their values were very different. Athens prized art, philosophy, and public debate, and it developed an early form of democracy in which male citizens voted on laws. Sparta, unlike Athens, focused almost entirely on military strength. Spartan boys began strict army training at age seven, while Athenian boys studied reading, music, and athletics.

parts.answer: Both were Greek city-states that fought Persia

parts.answer: Citizens voted on laws

passages.title: Water for Rome
passages.text: As ancient Rome grew to around one million people, it faced a serious problem: the Tiber River and local wells could not supply enough clean water. To solve this, Roman engineers built aqueducts, channels that carried water from distant springs into the city. The engineers gave each aqueduct a slight downward slope, and gravity pulled the water along without pumps. Where valleys blocked the route, they built tall stone bridges with arches. As a result, Rome had public fountains, baths, and toilets, and one aqueduct still carries water today.

parts.label: Problem
options: Rome did not have enough clean water
The Tiber River flooded the city
parts.answer: Rome did not have enough clean water

parts.label: Solution

parts.label: Result

passages.title: Gift of the Nile
passages.text: Each summer, heavy rains in the Ethiopian highlands caused the Nile River to flood. As the floodwaters spread across the valley in ancient Egypt, they left behind a layer of dark, rich soil called silt. Because this soil was so fertile, farmers could grow large crops of wheat and barley. As a result, Egypt produced extra food, which allowed some people to work as builders, scribes, and artisans instead of farmers. Therefore, the yearly flood helped make one of the world's great civilizations possible.

parts.label: Cause
parts.answer: The Nile flooded each summer

parts.label: Effect
options: Rich soil was left on the land
parts.answer: Rich soil was left on the land

parts.label: Another effect
parts.answer: Egypt grew extra food

passages.title: What a Histogram Shows
passages.text: A histogram is a graph that shows how a set of data is spread out. One feature that sets it apart from a bar graph is that its bars touch. Each bar stands for a range of numbers, called an interval, such as 10 to 19 or 20 to 29. The height of a bar shows the frequency, or how many data values fall in that interval. In addition, a histogram reveals the overall shape of the data. For example, it can show whether most values cluster in the middle or pile up at one end.

passages.title: Mean and Median
passages.text: The mean and the median are both measures of center. Each one uses a single number to describe a typical value in a data set. However, they are found in different ways. To find the mean, you add all the values and divide by how many values there are. To find the median, you put the values in order and choose the middle one. Unlike the median, the mean is strongly affected by an outlier, a value much higher or lower than the rest. The median, on the other hand, usually changes very little.

options: Both are found by choosing the middle value
parts.answer: Both describe a typical value

parts.answer: Add all the values and divide

passages.title: A Fair Survey
passages.text: The student council at Lincoln Middle School wanted to know which new club students preferred. At first, council members asked only their friends at lunch. This created a problem: the results showed what one small group thought, not the whole school. To solve the problem, the council used a random sample. They put every student's name in a computer list and randomly selected 60 names from all three grades. Each selected student answered the same short survey. As a result, the data represented the school more fairly, and the council chose a robotics club.

parts.answer: Only the council's friends were asked

passages.title: From Wind to Wire
passages.text: A wind turbine turns moving air into electricity in a series of steps. First, wind pushes against the long blades and makes them spin. Next, the spinning blades turn a shaft connected to a gearbox, which increases the speed of rotation. Then the fast-turning shaft drives a generator, where magnets and coils of copper wire produce an electric current. After that, cables carry the electricity down the tower to a transformer. Finally, the power travels through transmission lines to homes, schools, and businesses.

parts.answer: Wind makes the blades spin

passages.title: Solar and Wind Power
passages.text: Solar power and wind power are similar in several important ways. Both are renewable, meaning they will not run out, and both produce electricity without releasing smoke or carbon dioxide. However, they depend on different natural conditions. Solar panels generate electricity only when sunlight reaches them, and they produce nothing at night. Wind turbines, on the other hand, can run day or night, but they need steady wind. Unlike solar panels, which can fit on the roof of a house, large wind turbines usually stand in open fields or offshore.

parts.answer: Both are renewable and make no smoke

passages.title: Fossil Fuels and a Warming Planet
passages.text: When power plants burn coal, oil, or natural gas, they release carbon dioxide into the air. Because carbon dioxide traps heat near Earth's surface, adding more of it makes the planet warmer. Since the late 1800s, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen sharply. As a result, Earth's average temperature has increased, glaciers are melting, and sea levels are rising. Therefore, many countries are shifting toward cleaner energy sources to slow these changes.

parts.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide
